method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

supports: Handling contaminated linen with minimal agitation
PPE, contaminated equipment and clean preparation principles
sourceChecks.scope: Retrieved full primary guideline; targeted principles rather than all-item validation

supports: Closed-system protection and aseptic correction after disconnection

items.assessment: Point-of-use containment without agitation addresses contaminated linen spread; the incorrect transport and rinsing practices are recognizable workflow errors.
Containing the leak is correct, but parking it beside clean supplies and compressing leaking waste are cartoon alternatives.
issues: Containing the leak is correct, but parking it beside clean supplies and compressing leaking waste are cartoon alternatives.
proposedChanges: Use plausible competing containment/transport actions such as overbagging, transferring contents, continuing to the waste area, or first cleaning visible floor contamination. Make containment before movement decisive.

items.assessment: Premature drying fails the labelled wet contact time; label-directed reapplication is appropriate without inventing a universal duration.
Cleaning visible soil before disinfection is correct; sterilizing the entire cart is irrelevant and storage until dry is too weak.
issues: Cleaning visible soil before disinfection is correct; sterilizing the entire cart is irrelevant and storage until dry is too weak.
proposedChanges: Use parallel device-processing actions such as extra disinfectant, water rinse, cleaning according to instructions, or repeating the disinfection cycle. Explain cleaning versus disinfection distinctly.

items.assessment: Fresh cleaning materials are appropriate, but perfume and moving furniture closer to the toilet are nonclinical filler.
issues: Fresh cleaning materials are appropriate, but perfume and moving furniture closer to the toilet are nonclinical filler.
proposedChanges: Replace with plausible workflow errors such as reusing a visually clean portion, rinsing the cloth in the same bucket, or rewetting with product. Preserve dirty-to-clean contamination learning.

items.assessment: Verified chemical identification is correct; smell, appearance and extra volume form an overly obvious safety rule with little applied context.
issues: Verified chemical identification is correct; smell, appearance and extra volume form an overly obvious safety rule with little applied context.
proposedChanges: Either label foundation honestly or add a realistic time-pressure/preparation scenario and competing verification/cleanup actions. Avoid making all alternatives simply guess the liquid.

items.assessment: The concept that dedicated equipment still requires cleaning is useful, but this repeats three generalized good actions against explicitly skipping hand hygiene.
issues: The concept that dedicated equipment still requires cleaning is useful, but this repeats three generalized good actions against explicitly skipping hand hygiene.
proposedChanges: Use a concrete commode-cleaning scenario with two or three clinically relevant selections among five, including realistic misconceptions about dedication, splash protection or cleaning frequency.

items.assessment: Single-use labelling and approved processing instructions should govern use; appearance, hand rub and matching diagnosis do not authorize improvised reuse.
Damp packaging compromises the sterile barrier despite being unopened; drying, inspection and smaller wound size do not restore assurance.
An unattended unobserved field lacks sterility assurance; covering or replacing only an edge cannot resolve unknown contamination.
Avoiding nonsterile reach-over is correct, but the key is much longer and states its own rationale.
issues: Avoiding nonsterile reach-over is correct, but the key is much longer and states its own rationale.
proposedChanges: Shorten the key to Reposition supplies or obtain assistance and keep the nonsterile-clothing explanation in the rationale. Use similarly concise procedural alternatives.

items.assessment: A bed rail is nonsterile even after cleaning, so the contaminated sterile glove must be replaced before invasive-device contact.
Protocol-guided aseptic replacement after closed-system disconnection is correct; leaving it open until emptying is a cartoon distractor.
issues: Protocol-guided aseptic replacement after closed-system disconnection is correct; leaving it open until emptying is a cartoon distractor.
proposedChanges: Replace the open-system option with changing the drainage bag and reconnecting the original catheter; explain guideline-based replacement of catheter and collection system after a compromised connection.

items.assessment: Both floor contamination and elevated-bag backflow require correction; partial positioning fixes, emptying and routine clamping are plausible insufficient alternatives.
Procedure completion triggers review of catheter necessity, continued closed-system care and authorized removal; routine disconnection is an authentic common error.
A disinfected sampling port preserves the system and provides a suitable culture specimen, but floor-spill collection is implausible.
issues: A disinfected sampling port preserves the system and provides a suitable culture specimen, but floor-spill collection is implausible.
proposedChanges: Replace floor-spill collection with a realistic wrong access method such as puncturing nondesignated catheter tubing; specify use of the designated port according to device instructions.

items.assessment: A sink used for dirty equipment is an inappropriate injection-preparation location; smaller batches or local wiping do not create adequate clean separation.
Fresh sterile needle/syringe plus stopper disinfection is correct; key length gives away the only fully specified action.
issues: Fresh sterile needle/syringe plus stopper disinfection is correct; key length gives away the only fully specified action.
proposedChanges: Shorten the key to Disinfect the stopper and use new sterile equipment, retaining needle and syringe detail in the rationale, and align alternative lengths.

items.assessment: Removing the contaminated shared vial and reporting is sound; reserving it for the next client is an implausible salvage strategy.
issues: Removing the contaminated shared vial and reporting is sound; reserving it for the next client is an implausible salvage strategy.
proposedChanges: Use Reserve it for the client whose syringe entered it as the misconception, explaining that this does not authorize salvage of a contaminated shared vial.

items.assessment: The marked fill line gives an objective replacement trigger; overfilling, loose storage and manipulating contents increase sharps exposure.
A visible needle in linen requires controlled approved retrieval rather than shaking, manual pickup through gloves or transferring risk to laundry staff.
Immediate eye irrigation is correct, but alcohol and a dry dressing are cartoon responses and the key uniquely bundles follow-up.
issues: Immediate eye irrigation is correct, but alcohol and a dry dressing are cartoon responses and the key uniquely bundles follow-up.
proposedChanges: Compare appropriate exposure tasks by priority: immediate irrigation, contacting occupational health, notifying the supervisor, or arranging source assessment. Explain irrigation before subsequent coordination.

items.assessment: Arranging safe disposal before injection prevents avoidable recapping and transport of an exposed sharp; the plan is clear and within routine nursing safety.
Containment and laboratory guidance are correct; combining blood specimens with food samples is unrelated filler.
issues: Containment and laboratory guidance are correct; combining blood specimens with food samples is unrelated filler.
proposedChanges: Replace the food-bag option with placing the leaking original tube into a new specimen bag; explain why containment does not establish specimen integrity or suitability for analysis.

items.assessment: The item appropriately asks for local IPAC handling rather than inventing a universal rule for all room-exposed unopened supplies; outer contamination and package compatibility are distinguished.
